sn.headline: Louga police seize 7 kg of cannabis
sn.dek: Two men were arrested in Moukh Moukh with 7 kilograms of Indian hemp and other items.
paragraphs: The Louga regional drug brigade arrested two individuals and seized 7 kilograms of Indian hemp in Moukh Moukh, a village 52 kilometers from Louga. The operation followed intelligence about a suspected cannabis trafficking network. Police intercepted the suspects on a dirt road leading to Diewal village, finding five blocks of cannabis in their bag. A motorcycle they used was also impounded.

Further searches at the suspects' homes uncovered two additional blocks of cannabis, each weighing one kilogram, hidden in a plastic bucket at the first suspect's residence. Investigators also found two cartons containing a total of 21 bottles of whisky. The total seizure included seven blocks of cannabis, mobile phones, and a Jakarta-type motorcycle.

The two arrested individuals were taken to the service headquarters for questioning as part of the ongoing investigation. The total weight of the seized cannabis was confirmed at 7 kilograms after weighing.

sn.headline: Senegal forum links sport, health, and agriculture
sn.dek: African food systems forum in Dakar highlights maternal health and nutrition challenges.
paragraphs: The African food systems forum, held on October 30 at the Museum of Black Civilizations in Dakar, brought together public officials, athletes, and youth to discuss maternal, neonatal, and child health, alongside nutrition.

Amath Pathé Sène, director general of the forum, stressed the connection between agriculture, diet, and athletic performance, stating, "We are what we eat." Cathy Fall Sow of the Gates Foundation noted that nearly 70% of the 700 daily global maternal deaths occur in Africa, urging young people and athletes to become health ambassadors.

Dr. Ibrahima Hathie, representing the agriculture minister, emphasized agriculture's role in improving nutrition and called for climate-resilient food systems. Dr. Amadou Doucouré, director of Mother and Child Health, highlighted persistent challenges and the need for cross-sectoral collaboration, including sports figures raising awareness.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone charcoal burning causes deforestation
sl.dek: The practice of burning wood for charcoal is destroying economic trees and threatening food security, officials say.
paragraphs: Charcoal burning is a common source of livelihood in Sierra Leone, particularly in Freetown, as only 36% of the population has access to electricity and 15% to clean cooking.

The Environmental Protection Agency acknowledged the practice's hazards, noting that burners are cutting down fruit trees like orange and mango, leaving land exposed to climate change and threatening food security.
Greenhouse gas emissions from charcoal production and use contribute to climate change, which could reduce future wood supplies, according to the Food and Agricultural Organization.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone students face withheld exam results
sl.dek: One in four candidates had results withheld for suspected malpractice, fewer than one in 10 passed English.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone's 2026 West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE) results show that 47,454 candidates had their results withheld for suspected malpractice. The Minister of Basic and Senior Secondary Education, Mr Conrad Sackey, announced the results on Tuesday, October 27, 2026.

The Justice Reform Initiative-SL (JRI-SL) has condemned the mass withholding of results, calling it a threat to students' academic futures and university admission chances. The organisation gave the West African Examinations Council (WAEC) and the Ministry of Basic and Senior Secondary Education (MBSSE) a 21-day ultimatum to address the issue or face legal action.

JRI-SL urged WAEC and MBSSE to establish a transparent verification process for alleged infractions and release results for candidates without direct evidence of cheating. The organisation also called for a national dialogue on recurring concerns about student performance in English Language.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone vice presidents fail to reach presidency
sl.dek: The constitution grants power, but political appointments sideline vice presidents from leadership.
paragraphs: In Sierra Leone, the Vice Presidency, constitutionally powerful, has historically served as a political cul-de-sac. Since independence, no Vice President has been elected President, raising questions about the current officeholder's fate. Vice Presidents are often appointed to balance regional, religious, or ethnic considerations, appease party blocs, neutralize rivals, or reward loyalty, rather than cultivate ambition.

This practice means most Vice Presidents enter office without a clear succession pathway or an independent political base. Examples include Sorie Ibrahim Koroma and Francis Minah under Siaka Stevens, and Solomon Ekuma Berewa, who lost the 2007 presidential election despite extensive experience. Victor Bockarie Foh's short tenure and Samuel Sam-Sumana's expulsion from his party also illustrate the office's political precarity.

The 1991 Constitution intended the Vice Presidency to ensure continuity and executive depth. However, successive governments have treated it as a political balancing mechanism. This has led to a pattern where proximity to power does not translate into political security or a viable path to the presidency.

sl.headline: Female artisanal miners report sexual violence in Kono district mines
sl.dek: Women working in diamond-rich pits in Jaiama Nimikor face systemic rape and harassment while struggling to earn a living in Sierra Leone.
paragraphs: Women scavenging for gold and diamonds in the Jaiama Nimikor mining area of Kono district report frequent incidents of rape and sexual harassment. Janet, a 32-year-old miner, stated she was raped at age 15 while working alone in a pit eight miles from Koidu. She became pregnant following the assault and faced community stigmatization, eventually losing custody of her child to a relative.

Haja, a 48-year-old widow and mother of three, said she was also raped while working in the mines. She reported the assault to a camp master, who dismissed her claim by alleging the attacker was her boyfriend. Haja fled to the village of Guitor to escape the shame of the incident, leaving her children behind before eventually returning to her community.

Many women turned to artisanal mining to support their families following the end of the civil war in Sierra Leone. These miners often work in abandoned pits to find gold or diamonds after dropping out of school or losing their spouses. Despite reporting these crimes to village authorities and camp officials, victims say they have received little to no support or justice for the violence they endure.

so.headline: UN mission in Somalia closes after 30 years
so.dek: The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) ceased operations on Saturday, ending a long UN presence.
paragraphs: The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) officially closed on Saturday, concluding over three decades of UN operations in the nation at the Somali government's request. This closure finalizes a two-year transition period mandated by Security Council resolutions 2753 (2024) and 2809 (2025). UNTMIS's functions have now been transferred to Somali institutions and various UN agencies, funds, and programmes.

UN Secretary-General spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric stated that the UN commends the Somali people's determination and acknowledges remaining political, security, humanitarian, and development challenges. The UN will continue its work in Somalia through resident agencies, funds, and programmes, collaborating with Somali authorities, the African Union, and international partners. Raisedon Zenenga, the mission’s officer-in-charge, described the closure as the start of a new partnership chapter.

A farewell ceremony took place in Mogadishu on October 26, attended by Zenenga and Deputy Prime Minister Salah Ahmed Jama, who called the closure a "day of victory." UN missions in Somalia date back to 1992, with UNTMIS succeeding UNSOM, which began in June 2013. The mission's closure occurs amidst a sharp decline in funding for Somalia.

so.headline: Uganda begins Somalia troop pullout after 20 years
so.dek: The first contingent of 109 soldiers departed Mogadishu airport on Friday, marking the start of a withdrawal.
paragraphs: Uganda has started withdrawing its troops from Somalia after two decades of fighting Al-Shabaab. A Kenya-registered aircraft chartered by Uganda departed Mogadishu airport on Friday carrying 109 soldiers, the first group to leave. Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni informed Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud of his decision to withdraw forces before November 15, rejecting Mohamud’s request to delay the pullout.

Ugandan forces, stationed in the Lower Shabelle region, are set to hand over forward operating bases to the Somali army by November 4. Uganda first deployed troops in 2007, helping to drive Al-Shabaab from Mogadishu and other key towns. Their departure from river-crossing towns vital to Mogadishu’s security raises questions about the capital’s future safety.

Uganda People's Defence Force chief General Muhoozi Kainerugaba announced the withdrawal on Thursday, stating, “After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice we are handing over security to our Somali brothers.” The withdrawal follows President Museveni's rejection of President Mohamud's plea for a delay during a visit to Uganda on Monday, October 26.

so.headline: Fugitive rescues 40 Somali soldiers
so.dek: Duqow, sentenced to death, provided food and guided stranded troops to safety in Lower Shabelle.
paragraphs: A fugitive named Duqow rescued over 40 Somali Federal Government soldiers who were stranded for two nights in the Jameeco area of the Lower Shabelle region. The soldiers had become lost following a battle with Al-Shabaab militants. Duqow and local Macawiisley fighters found the disoriented troops, gave them food, and led them to the safety of Yaaqbiriweyne district.

Duqow, who has been on the run for nearly a year and was sentenced to death by military court judge Judge Shuute, denied disarming the soldiers. He stated he hosted them, provided refreshments, and contacted their commander to report their situation. Duqow expressed love for his government, saying, "The federal government is my government and I have no intention of seeking revenge."

The Somali Federal Government has not yet officially commented on the incident, leaving Duqow's legal standing and the military's response uncertain. Duqow has been actively sought by state security forces for execution of his sentence.

ss.headline: Juba City Council digitizes revenue collection
ss.dek: The council arrested 32 employees and launched a public website to improve financial transparency.
paragraphs: Juba City Council has launched a new digital financial payment system and a public website to improve transparency in revenue collection and fund management. Caretaker Mayor Christopher Sarafino Wani Swaka announced on Friday that the council has migrated all revenue operations from manual forms to a digitized system over the past 10 days.

Investigations uncovered financial malpractices, with Mayor Swaka stating that 50 percent of the council’s resources were lost. This led to the arrest of 32 revenue collectors who are facing disciplinary action, including potential dismissal. The reforms follow complaints from residents and business owners about the transparency of taxes and fees.

The council also launched a website, www.jccgov.ss, to provide public access to information like the annual budget and tax schedules. Mayor Swaka said this aims to address public uncertainty about fees and improve communication between the city and its residents.

ss.headline: UK gives South Sudan $2.8 million for flood preparedness
ss.dek: Funding will support early warning systems and aid for communities in Jonglei, Unity, and Upper Nile states.
paragraphs: The United Kingdom has provided 2.8 million US dollars to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme to help vulnerable communities in South Sudan prepare for climate-related disasters. The funding will support early flood preparedness and response activities in Jonglei, Unity, and Upper Nile states. The programme will provide early-warning information, cash assistance, livelihood support, community public works, and emergency supplies.

UK Development Director Sebastian Fouquet stated that climate shocks are worsening the country’s humanitarian situation, and acting on early warnings helps families protect their assets. WFP Country Director Mutinta Chimuka said early action is essential to prevent predictable climate shocks from becoming humanitarian emergencies. FAO Acting Representative Felix Dzvurumi added that the support will help farmers, livestock keepers, and fishing communities protect their livelihoods and improve food security.

The programme will run until March 2027 and will also strengthen community-based early-warning systems and coordination with government authorities. This contribution brings the UK’s total funding for El Niño-related early action in South Sudan to over £2.85 million. The initiative aims to reduce losses and protect livelihoods before disasters strike.

ss.headline: SSPDF reunites two abducted children with parents in Juba
ss.dek: Two-year-old Abi Gatwich Tuach and five-year-old Simon Gattiek Tut Kai were recovered from Gumuruk Town.
paragraphs: The South Sudan People’s Defense Forces (SSPDF) reunited two abducted children with their parents in Juba on Thursday. The handover ceremony occurred at the army headquarters in Bilpam. The children, Abi Gatwich Tuach, aged two, and Simon Gattiek Tut Kai, aged five, were recovered from Gumuruk Town in the Greater Pibor Administrative Area (GPAA).

SSPDF spokesperson Major General Lul Ruai Koang stated Abi was abducted on December 5, 2025, from Suk Darfur, and Simon on June 13, 2026, from Suk Arnab in Juba. He identified Juma Logocho, Ayella Dominic Onono, and Angok Ayok as alleged traffickers who sold the children to Mary Amei and Thomei Agany. The operation involved SSPDF intelligence and GPAA authorities.

Gen. Ruai reported that 32 missing children have been registered, with only three recovered so far. He appealed to the public to report missing children and provide information on suspected traffickers. The GPAA authorities were urged to intensify efforts to arrest remaining suspects and find other abducted children.

ss.headline: Kiir returns to Juba after Russia summit
ss.dek: Russia increased scholarship places for South Sudanese students to 40 for the 2026-2027 academic year.
paragraphs: South Sudanese President Salva Kiir returned to Juba on Saturday after attending the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow. During the summit, Russian President Vladimir Putin announced an increase in scholarship allocations for South Sudanese students to 40 places for the 2026-2027 academic year.

Putin stated that Russia would continue to assist in training personnel for South Sudan, noting that the two countries marked 15 years of diplomatic relations this year. He also mentioned exploring ways to strengthen bilateral trade and economic engagement, acknowledging that the full potential of their relationship had not yet been realised. The summit, which concluded on Thursday, October 29, saw participation from 48 African countries.

On the sidelines of the summit, South Sudan and Russia signed a Memorandum of Understanding and a Letter of Acceptance for the transfer of former Petronas shares in the Dar Petroleum Operating Company and Greater Pioneer Operating Company to Russia's Zarubezhneft. President Kiir had earlier invited Russian and other foreign investors to South Sudan, highlighting opportunities in agriculture, petroleum, mining, and tourism.

ss.headline: Stephen Dhieu wins SPLM gubernatorial primaries in Upper Nile
ss.dek: Dhieu secured 120 votes, defeating former governor Jacob Dollar and becoming the party's flag bearer for December 2026 elections.
paragraphs: Stephen Dhieu Dau won the SPLM gubernatorial primaries in Upper Nile State with 120 votes, becoming the party’s candidate for the December 2026 elections. SPLM Secretary-General Dr Akol Paul Kordit also named Dhieu the party’s chairperson for Upper Nile State. 13 candidates competed for the nomination.

Dhieu defeated former Upper Nile Governor Jacob Dollar, who received 12 votes, and East African Legislative Assembly Member of Parliament Kim Gai, who got three votes. The sole female aspirant, Advocate Ferida Philip Nyanan, received two votes. Gabriel Isaac came second with 38 votes and was confirmed as the deputy SPLM chairperson.

The primaries were supervised by a high-level SPLM National Leadership delegation led by Third Deputy Chairperson Simon Kun Puoch and Secretary-General Dr Akol Paul Kordit. The congress aimed to elect new state leadership and organise party structures ahead of the general elections.

sd.headline: RSF drones hit 12 power stations across Sudan
sd.dek: Rapid Support Forces attacks since Monday have damaged transformers and fuel installations, causing widespread blackouts.
paragraphs: Rapid Support Forces (RSF) drone attacks have crippled Sudan’s electricity network since Monday, knocking out power stations in at least six states. The strikes have damaged transformers, transmission equipment, and fuel installations from eastern Sudan to the capital, Khartoum. The Sudan Electricity Holding Company reported that the RSF targeted vital substations including Singa, Al-Hawata, Al-Faw, Mashkur, and Al-Geneid, causing extensive destruction and a complete blackout across the southeastern grid.

Witnesses reported explosions at the Abu Hamad facility, and the attacks have affected installations hundreds of kilometers from RSF ground positions. The electricity company stated these "treacherous terrorist attacks" pose a direct threat to the national grid's stability. The bombardment includes strikes on the Al Markhiyat substation northwest of Omdurman, cutting power to large parts of Khartoum.

Attacks have also hit Al Managil, Haya, and Rabak, following an earlier disruption at Tendelti electricity station. In Al Faw and Al Hawata, strikes affected facilities supplying towns and agricultural communities, impacting water pumping, irrigation, and commercial activities.

sd.headline: Sudan leader risks repeating Bashir's Russia gambit, analyst warns
sd.dek: Journalist Rasha Awad says Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's overtures to Moscow echo failed policies of the past.
paragraphs: Sudanese journalist Rasha Awad warned that military leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan is repeating former president Omar al-Bashir's strategy by seeking Russian political and economic support. Burhan's recent engagement with Moscow, including proposals for investment in mining and infrastructure, mirrors al-Bashir's past efforts to deepen ties with Russia. Al-Bashir visited Russia in November 2017 and sought protection against American actions.

Awad told Radio Tamazuj on Saturday that al-Bashir's previous reliance on Russia did not prevent his overthrow in April 2019. She stated that Burhan's current diplomatic moves are a reaction to his failure to achieve peace and his lack of cooperation with international efforts led by the United States. Awad believes Burhan is using the prospect of closer ties with Moscow as a political maneuver to counter Western pressure and consolidate his power.

However, Awad cautioned that this strategy is unlikely to succeed due to competing international and regional interests. She questioned Russia's ability to provide the expected support, citing Russia's military presence in Syria which did not prevent Bashar al-Assad's rule from collapsing in December 2024. Awad noted that Moscow's broader interests with the United States and Gulf countries could limit its willingness to offer unconditional backing to Sudan's military authorities.

sd.headline: South Sudan election order reversed
sd.dek: Elections are now scheduled for December 22 under the transitional constitution, reversing the agreed order for a permanent constitution first.
paragraphs: South Sudan's planned elections, scheduled for December 22, will now proceed under the transitional constitution. This decision reverses the order previously set by the 2018 peace agreement, which stipulated elections should occur after a permanent constitution was established.

Regina Adyeng Amaylek Amuch, who fled to Khartoum in 2013 and returned to Malakal this year, stated that lasting peace is what she needs most. She expressed this in August to the United Nations, highlighting the fragility of her rebuilt life and the constant threat of displacement.

The current approach has been criticized for asking citizens to choose election referees before agreeing on the rules of the game. Previous attempts to settle power-sharing, including agreements in 2005, 2015, and 2018, focused on dividing offices rather than defining the country's governance terms.

sd.headline: Sudan displaced face food, medicine shortages
sd.dek: Around 27,400 people in Blue Nile region lack basic supplies amid disease and calls for aid.
paragraphs: Displaced people in Sudan’s Blue Nile region are facing severe shortages of food and medicine, alongside disease outbreaks and a lack of educational and employment opportunities. The Blue Nile Humanitarian Aid Commissioner, Gisma Abdel-Karim, stated that efforts are underway to provide immediate aid, including food and shelter, in coordination with humanitarian partners.

The World Food Programme is supplying food baskets, ADRA is providing cash assistance, and Islamic Relief is distributing hygiene kits to approximately 10,600 pregnant and breastfeeding women. However, Issa Khamis, displaced from Balaro, reported that the assistance is insufficient, with ongoing struggles due to food scarcity and disease spread.

Al-Radhiya Arbab, a mother of 12 displaced from Kurmuk locality, called for improved healthcare and medicine availability, and for children to be enrolled in school. Displaced families from Kurmuk are experiencing worsening hunger, and a committee member requested employment for young people to alleviate family financial pressures.

tg.headline: Togo party welcomes ECOWAS court letter on constitutional order
tg.dek: The Santé du Peuple party urged a swift return to the 1992 constitution, rejecting academic discussions.
paragraphs: The Santé du Peuple party in Togo, led by Dr Georges WILLIAM-KOUESSAN, has welcomed a letter sent on October 23, 2026, by the ECOWAS Court of Justice to the Togolese Minister of Justice. This letter demands the execution of the court's January 29, 2026 ruling, which declared unconstitutional a constitutional change made two years prior.

In a statement dated October 30, 2026, the party expressed satisfaction with the ECOWAS court's action. They are calling on Togolese authorities for a "rapid and peaceful" return to the 1992 constitutional order. The party also stated that academic discussions cannot resolve the current crisis.

The Santé du Peuple party's reaction follows the ECOWAS court's demand for the enforcement of its January 29, 2026, ruling. The party believes this ruling invalidates the constitutional changes implemented in Togo over the past two years.

The organization urged the courts to re-examine the case and lift the judicial control unless a legal and proportionate necessity justifies its continuation. UJPLA highlighted the importance of protecting press freedom and the public's right to information.

tg.headline: African consumers urge zero added sugar for young children
tg.dek: The African Consumers Organisation (OAC) is pushing for new international standards to remove added sugars from infant foods.
paragraphs: The African Consumers Organisation (OAC) is urging African nations to support a goal of zero added sugar in foods for children aged 6 to 36 months. This call comes as the 45th session of the Codex Committee on Nutrition approaches. The OAC, representing 50 consumer groups across 39 African countries, wants to protect children's health from an early age.

An investigation by Public Eye found that Cerelac infant cereals, popular in Africa, contain nearly six grams of added sugar per serving, unlike European versions. The OAC asked Nestlé on June 25, 2026, to remove added sugar from its African products. Nestlé responded on July 20, 2026, stating its products meet national regulations and Codex Standard CXS 74-1981, and that it now offers versions with and without added sugar.

The current Codex standard allows up to 20% added sugar in infant cereals, equivalent to about 10 grams per portion. The World Health Organization warns that early sugar exposure can lead to a lasting preference for sweet foods and obesity, which is rising alarmingly in Africa. The OAC is advocating for changes at the standards level to ensure child protection.

tg.headline: Lycée Adidogomé 1 beats Lycée Zébévi in Génie Imhotep

paragraphs: Lycée Adidogomé 1 defeated Lycée Zébévi on Saturday, October 31, 2026, in the fourth round of the third season of the 'Génie Imhotep' quiz competition. The match took place at the Prof James studio of SOS Docteur TV in Lomé.

Students from Lycée Zébévi, located in the Lacs prefecture, scored 370 points, while their counterparts from Lycée Adidogomé 1, from the Grand Lomé region, achieved 410 points. This loss follows a narrow victory for Zébévi against Tokoin 2 the previous week.

This third edition of the competition, supported by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and promoted by Professor Serge Michel Kodom of Aimes-Afrique, now includes six schools from the Maritime region alongside six from Lomé. The next match will feature Lycée Adidogomé 1 against Lycée Attitogon.

tn.headline: Tunis court sentences neighbour to death for child murder
tn.dek: A young man will be hanged for strangling a six-year-old girl and hiding her body on a neighbour's roof in 2025.
paragraphs: A criminal court in Tunis has sentenced a young man to death by hanging for the premeditated murder of his six-year-old neighbour. The court found the man guilty of strangling the child with a sock in 2025. He then wrapped her body in curtain fabric and hid it on a neighbour's roof.

The crime began with the girl's disappearance, causing distress to her family and neighbours in the El Omrane El Aala district. Investigations led to the neighbour, known to the victim and other children in the area. He admitted to luring the girl to his home after she returned alone.

The court's decision followed the examination of the case and the evidence presented. The convicted man had previously hidden at a friend's house in Ettadhamen after the murder. The body was discovered shortly after being concealed on the roof.

tn.headline: Tunisia braces for thunderstorms and strong winds

Winds will blow from the north, becoming strong near the coasts and on the highlands. The sea will be rough to very rough along the northern coasts, requiring special attention for maritime activities. Temperatures will range from 15 to 21°C in the north and west, and 21 to 24°C elsewhere.

The INM also reported scattered, stormy rain in the north and south, with very cloudy skies in some parts. The Gulf of Hammamet will see rough seas, while other coasts will be less agitated. Overnight temperatures are predicted between 9 and 13°C in western regions and 14 to 18°C in the rest of the country.

tn.headline: Tunisia transport attacks cost 4 million dinars
tn.dek: Attacks on trains, metros, and buses in 2025-2026 damaged property and affected 362 people, according to the transport minister.
paragraphs: Attacks on public transport in Tunisia caused approximately 4 million dinars in material damage during 2025-2026, stated Transport Minister Rachid Amri. The minister also reported that 362 individuals, including drivers and sector agents, were affected by these incidents. Amri presented these figures on Saturday, October 31, in Ben Arous during a meeting focused on preserving public transport services.

The reported cost covers damage to multiple public transport vehicles, with no detailed breakdown provided for specific operators or the two years involved. Minister Amri noted that these expenses could have funded other developments within the transport sector. For example, replacing broken train windows due to thrown stones in 2025 alone cost the SNCFT around 162,000 dinars, a figure separate from the 4 million dinar total which covers broader damages across networks.

Beyond material repairs, Amri highlighted the disruption these attacks cause to passengers, impacting their ability to reach work, appointments, or medical facilities. The SNCFT has also emphasized the risks posed by stone-throwing incidents to both passengers and staff. To address these issues, a collective prevention strategy involving families, schools, and civil society has been proposed to protect transport infrastructure and personnel.

zm.headline: Zambia plans orderly urban growth
zm.dek: Vice-President Nalumango says urban planning must improve services without displacing people.
paragraphs: Vice-President Mutale Nalumango stated that urban planning in Zambia must address community needs by enhancing access to basic services while avoiding unnecessary displacement of people and their livelihoods. She announced the government's commitment to fostering orderly human settlements, upgrading infrastructure, and expanding economic prospects as urban areas grow. Minister of Local Government and Rural Development Gift Sialubalo delivered the speech on her behalf at the National Urban Conference in Lusaka.

Mrs Nalumango emphasized that urban development should be inclusive and practical, ensuring planning leads to better living conditions for citizens. She noted that challenges like unplanned settlements, poor drainage, sanitation, housing congestion, and insecurity require coordinated planning and infrastructure investment. Land allocation and investment decisions should be guided by spatial planning and supported by essential infrastructure such as roads, water, schools, and health facilities.

The government is also promoting decentralisation to move decision-making closer to communities, with local authorities tasked to translate development priorities into actionable plans and projects. Integrated development plans are important in guiding local investments, and national institutions are urged to align their support with local authority priorities. Chief Chamuka called for stronger collaboration between traditional leaders, local authorities, and policymakers to manage urban expansion, especially in customary areas facing high land demand.

eh.dek: Moscow blocks changes to MINURSO mandate, citing an unbalanced approach to negotiations.
paragraphs: Russia vetoed a United States-led draft resolution on October 30, 2026, that aimed to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO). The decision by Moscow prevents the proposal from advancing in its current form and halts substantial changes to the mission's political and operational framework.

The US-backed resolution sought to rename MINURSO, removing the reference to a referendum, and to establish Morocco's autonomy plan as the primary negotiation framework. Russia stated the US text was unbalanced and could compromise the UN's impartiality in the political process, blocking the resolution's approval.

This veto creates a diplomatic setback for Washington, requiring them to revise their proposal to find an alternative that renews the mission's mandate without causing a diplomatic deadlock. The future of MINURSO and the international framework for resolving the Western Sahara conflict now faces renewed tension among Security Council members.

ls.headline: China reaffirms ties and multilateralism with Lesotho
ls.dek: Ambassador Yang Xiaokun urged local media to respect China's sovereignty claims over Taiwan.
paragraphs: Chinese Ambassador to Lesotho, Yang Xiaokun, met with local media in Maseru this week to reaffirm China's commitment to multilateralism and strengthening relations with Lesotho. The meeting marked the 55th anniversary of the restoration of the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC) seat at the United Nations (UN) and Commemoration Day of Taiwan’s Restoration.

Ambassador Yang stated that history shapes international relations and offers lessons for safeguarding peace and nations' legitimate rights. He recalled that the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758 on 25 October 1971, which restored the PRC's rights at the UN and recognised its representatives as the sole legitimate representatives of China.

The ambassador also highlighted China's contributions to international development and peace efforts, including its Global Development Initiative which has mobilised over US$23 billion. China has implemented zero-tariff treatment for 53 African countries, a measure from which Lesotho is expected to benefit.

ls.headline: Econet raises M971 000 for education fund
ls.dek: The annual Econet Golf Day and Expo gala dinner secured funds for vulnerable students in Lesotho.
paragraphs: Econet Telecom Lesotho (ETL) raised M971 000 for its HigherLife Foundation Lesotho through its annual golf day and gala dinner on Friday at Maseru Mall. The funds were generated from pledges and a matching contribution from ETL. The event also marked the conclusion of the fourth Econet Expo, themed “Think AI, Think Econet”.

ETL Chief Executive Officer Dennis Plaatjies stated that the golf day, established in 2018, supports the foundation's mission to uplift young Basotho through education. The foundation currently assists 141 tertiary students and 114 secondary students. Plaatjies explained that ETL allocates two percent of its annual revenue, approximately M13 million to M15 million, to the foundation, but additional fundraising is necessary due to growing needs.

A total of 84 golfers participated in the tournament. The winning team, comprising Tlotliso Khabo, Tsebo Lerotholi, Matšela Matšela, and Moeketsi Mafereka, finished with 58 points. The event's synergy with the ETL Expo allowed international partners to engage in business and personal networking.

ls.headline: Lesotho cricket team ends Nigeria campaign with defeat
ls.dek: The national side lost to Gambia by three runs, finishing fourth in the tournament standings.
paragraphs: Lesotho's campaign in the Africa Cricket Association regional qualifying tournament in Abuja concluded with a narrow three-run defeat against Gambia. The national team was bowled out for 109 in 19.5 overs while chasing Gambia's total of 112 for nine.

This result placed Lesotho fourth in the final standings, securing one win from five matches and accumulating two points. According to the Lesotho Cricket Association (LCA), Nigeria and Uganda advanced to the Africa Regional Final.

Coach Dzikamai Mavhiko highlighted the team's limitations, including the absence of a dedicated cricket ground and the challenge of competing against full-time players, stating that sustained investment in facilities and player development is necessary.

ls.headline: Lesotho government allocates M50 million for Royal Palace
ls.dek: The Senate's Committee on Government Assurances reports on the stalled M355 million palace project and overpayments.
paragraphs: The Lesotho government has allocated M50 million to restart construction of the new Royal Palace in Maseru. This project, initiated in 2011, has faced delays and cost overruns, now standing at M355 million.

A Senate Committee on Government Assurances report, based on the Auditor-General’s May 2025 audit, revealed overpayments exceeding M74 million to consultants and contractors. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport has developed a new procurement strategy to prevent future issues.
The ministry is preparing to resume construction soon, assuring the committee that corrective measures are in place. The initial project cost was M136.7 million, with completion expected in May 2013.

ls.headline: Lesotho names four players for AUSC Region 5 Games
ls.dek: Phuthi Leshoele, Lindiwe Nkanda, Thabo Chimombe, and Kamohelo Mathibela will compete in lawn tennis in Maputo, Mozambique.
paragraphs: The Lesotho Lawn Tennis Association (LLTA) has selected a four-member team for the upcoming African Union Sports Council (AUSC) Region 5 Games in Maputo, Mozambique, from December 4 to 13.

Phuthi Leshoele and Lindiwe Nkanda will play in the women's category, while Thabo Chimombe and Kamohelo Mathibela will compete in the men's category, coached by Bishop Mosebi and ‘Mankopane Nkuatsana. LLTA Public Relations Officer Mathealira Chaka confirmed the team's selection and ongoing preparations.

Lesotho will participate in only eight sporting codes due to financial constraints, missing disciplines like basketball and swimming, though visually impaired and Special Olympics athletes will compete in athletics.
